title: Building sentences
keyIdea: A sentence is a group of words that tells a complete thought. It says who or what (the dog) and what they do (runs). A bit with a piece missing, like 'The dog' or 'jumps high', is not a whole sentence yet. You can add details about where, when or how, and it is still one sentence. A written sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop.

kid: Words join up to make a sentence. A sentence tells a whole idea. 'The dog runs.' is a sentence.
A sentence needs two parts. Who is it about? The dog. What does it do? Runs. Put them together: The dog runs.
'The dog' is not finished. You want to ask, what does the dog do? 'jumps high' is not finished too. Who jumps?
You can make a sentence bigger. The cat sleeps on the mat. The cat sleeps all day. It is still one sentence. When you write it, start with a big capital letter. Stop with a full stop at the end.
adult: In England, Year 1 pupils learn how words combine to make sentences, using the terms word, sentence, capital letter, full stop and punctuation; US Common Core asks kindergarteners to produce and expand complete sentences in shared language activities (L.K.1f). The grammar underneath is a subject (who or what) plus a verb (what they do), which together express a complete thought.

The quickest test is to say it aloud and listen: if you are left asking 'who?' or 'what happened?', it is a fragment, not a sentence. 'The big red bus' names a thing but has no verb; 'ran to the park' has a verb but no subject. Children can often hear this before they can explain it, so talk comes first and writing second.

Common mistakes: treating any group of words as a sentence because it starts with a capital letter; thinking a longer sentence must be two sentences, and putting a full stop before an added detail ('The cat sleeps. On the mat.'); full stops after every word or line; and a lower-case first letter. Expanding with a where, when or how phrase keeps one subject and one verb, so it stays one sentence.

In the lab your child couples a who car and a doing car to make word trains, sorts whole sentences from unfinished bits, mends three fragments with the missing piece, stretches 'The cat sleeps.' with details, and adds the capital letter and the full stop.

familyTip: Play 'finish my sentence': say 'The cat…' and stop. Your child adds what the cat does. Swap: they start with a doing word ('…jumps!') and you add who. Then make it bigger together: where? when?

visual.caption: Is it a whole sentence, or not finished yet? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: couple who and doing-word cars into sentences, sort whole from unfinished, fix fragments, add details and put in the capital letter and full stop.

practice.prompt: Which one is a whole sentence?
practice.hint: A whole sentence says who, and what they do.
practice.explain: 'The cat naps.' says who (the cat) and what it does (naps). The others each miss a piece.

practice.prompt: There are {n} ducks. 'The {n} ducks' is not finished. What is missing?
practice.hint: We know who. Do we know what they do?
practice.explain: We know who: the {n} ducks. We do not know what they do, so add a doing word: The {n} ducks swim.

practice.prompt: 'jumps in the mud' is not finished. What is missing?
practice.hint: Jumps is the doing word. Who is doing it?
practice.explain: Jumps is the doing word, but we do not know who. Add a who: The pig jumps in the mud.

practice.prompt: Sam has {n} sentences to write. Where does the full stop go in each one?
practice.hint: The full stop tells you to stop.
practice.explain: A full stop goes at the end of each of the {n} sentences, after the last word.

pool.hint: Think about 'The dog runs.' It makes sense on its own.
pool.explain: A sentence tells a whole idea: who, and what they do. One word or a name is only a piece.

pool.prompt: Which one is NOT a whole sentence?
pool.hint: Look for the one with no doing word.
pool.explain: 'The big blue ball' names a thing, but it does not say what happens.

pool.hint: Add a doing word that says what the frog does.
pool.explain: 'hops' is a doing word, so 'The frog hops.' is whole. 'green' and 'the pond' do not say what it does.

pool.prompt: 'The {n} birds sing in the tree.' How many sentences is this?
pool.hint: Count the who and the doing words.
pool.explain: One. 'in the tree' is a detail about where. There is one who (the {n} birds) and one doing word (sing), so one sentence.

pool.prompt: Which one is written the right way?
pool.hint: Look at the start and the end.
pool.explain: It starts with a capital letter (The) and ends with a full stop.

pool.prompt: Mia makes {n} sentences. Each has a who. What else does each need?
pool.hint: A sentence has a who, and then what they do.
pool.explain: Each of the {n} sentences needs a doing word, to say what the who does.

pool.prompt: Add a detail to 'The dog runs.' Which is best?
choices: The dog runs in the park.
The dog runs. In the park.
pool.hint: Keep the detail inside the one sentence.
pool.explain: 'The dog runs in the park.' keeps one sentence. 'In the park.' on its own is not finished.
